title: Part 2, Chapter 62
paragraphs: Which recounts the adventure of the enchanted head, along with other trifling matters that cannot be left untold

Don Quixote's host was a man named Don Antonio Moreno, a gentleman of wealth and good sense who loved amusing himself in any decent, good-humored way; and now that he had Don Quixote under his roof, he began thinking up ways to draw out his madness without doing him any harm—for a joke that wounds is no joke at all, and no entertainment is worth having if it comes at someone else's expense. The first thing he did was have Don Quixote remove his armor and then parade him, in that snug chamois outfit we have already described and pictured more than once, out onto a balcony overlooking one of the city's main streets, in plain sight of the crowds and the boys, who stared at him as if he were a monkey on display. The riders in livery wheeled and pranced before him once again, as though they had put on their finery for him alone rather than to brighten that day's festival, and Sancho was beside himself with pleasure, because it seemed to him—he couldn't say how—that he had stumbled into another wedding like Camacho's, another house like Don Diego de Miranda's, another castle like the duke's. Several of Don Antonio's friends dined with him that day, and all of them paid honor to Don Quixote and treated him as a knight-errant, which so puffed him up and elevated him that he could hardly contain his satisfaction. As for Sancho, his witticisms were such that the entire household staff, and everyone else within earshot, hung on his every word. While they were at the table Don Antonio said to him, "We hear, good Sancho, that you are so fond of blancmange and meatballs that if any are left over, you tuck them into your shirt for the next day."

"No, señor, that's not true," said Sancho, "because I'm more tidy than greedy, and my master Don Quixote here knows perfectly well that the two of us are used to living for a week on a handful of acorns or walnuts. Of course, if it happens that somebody offers me a heifer, I come running with the halter—by which I mean, I eat what's put in front of me and take my chances as they come; but anyone who says I'm a sloppy eater or not clean about it, let me tell him he's got it wrong—and I'd put that more strongly if I didn't respect the honorable beards sitting at this table."

"Truly," said Don Quixote, "Sancho's restraint and cleanliness at the table deserve to be inscribed and engraved on plates of bronze, to be remembered forever in ages yet to come. It's true that when he's hungry there is a certain look of voracity about him, since he eats at a furious rate and chews with both sides of his jaw at once; but he never forgets his cleanliness, and during his time as governor he learned to eat with such delicacy that he takes his grapes, and even pomegranate seeds, with a fork."
"What!" said Don Antonio. "Sancho has been a governor?"

"Yes," said Sancho, "of an island called Barataria. I governed it to perfection for ten days, and lost my peace of mind the whole time, and learned to despise every government in the world. I got out of the place by running away, and fell into a pit where I gave myself up for dead, and only got out of it alive by a miracle."
Don Quixote then gave them a detailed account of the entire business of Sancho's governorship, which entertained his listeners enormously.

When the table was cleared, Don Antonio took Don Quixote by the hand and led him into a remote room whose only furnishing was a table, apparently of jasper, standing on a pedestal of the same material; on it was set a head, seemingly of bronze, in the style of the busts of the Roman emperors. Don Antonio walked Don Quixote through the whole apartment and circled the table with him several times, and then said, "Now, Señor Don Quixote, since I am satisfied that no one is listening and the door is shut, I am going to tell you about one of the rarest adventures—or rather, one of the strangest things—imaginable, on the condition that you keep what I say buried in the deepest vaults of secrecy."

"I swear it," said Don Quixote, "and for extra security I will lay a flagstone over it; for I would have you know, Señor Don Antonio" (by now he had learned his host's name), "that you are speaking to a man who has ears to hear but no tongue to tell, so you may safely pour whatever is in your breast into mine and trust that you have dropped it into the depths of silence itself."

"Trusting in that promise," said Don Antonio, "I will astonish you with what you are about to see and hear, and ease some of the frustration I feel at having no one to whom I can confide my secrets—for they are not the kind that can be trusted to just anyone."

Don Quixote was puzzled, wondering what could be the point of all these precautions; then Don Antonio took his hand and passed it over the bronze head and over the whole table and the jasper pedestal it stood on, and said, "This head, Señor Don Quixote, was made and constructed by one of the greatest magicians and sorcerers the world has ever known—a Pole by birth, I believe, and a pupil of the famous Escotillo about whom so many marvelous stories are told. He stayed here in my house, and for the sum of a thousand crowns that I paid him he built this head, which has the power and property of answering any question spoken into its ear. He plotted compass bearings, drew figures, studied the stars, watched for the favorable moments, and at last brought it to the perfection we shall witness tomorrow—for on Fridays it is mute, and since today is Friday we must wait until the next day. In the meantime your worship can think over what you would like to ask it; and I know from experience that everything it answers is the truth."

Don Quixote was astonished at the head's power and property, and was inclined not to believe Don Antonio; but seeing how little time he would have to wait before putting it to the test, he chose to say nothing except to thank him for revealing so great a secret. They then left the room, Don Antonio locked the door behind them, and they returned to the hall where the other gentlemen were gathered. In the meantime Sancho had been telling them about a number of the adventures and mishaps that had befallen his master.

That afternoon they took Don Quixote out for a ride, not in his armor but in town clothes, wearing a long coat of tawny cloth that, at that season, would have made ice itself break into a sweat. The servants were given orders to keep Sancho entertained so he wouldn't leave the house. Don Quixote rode not on Rocinante but on a tall, smooth-gaited mule with handsome trappings. They dressed him in the coat, and on his back, without his noticing, they pinned a parchment on which they had written in large letters, "This is Don Quixote of La Mancha." From the moment they set out, the sign drew the eyes of everyone who happened to pass, and as people read aloud, "This is Don Quixote of La Mancha," Don Quixote marveled that so many gazed at him, called him by name, and knew who he was; and turning to Don Antonio, who rode beside him, he remarked, "Great indeed are the privileges that come with knight-errantry, for it makes whoever practices it known and famous in every corner of the earth. Look, Don Antonio—even the very boys of this city know me, though they have never laid eyes on me before."

"True, Señor Don Quixote," replied Don Antonio, "for just as fire cannot be hidden or shut away, virtue cannot avoid being recognized; and the virtue won through the profession of arms shines out above every other kind."

But it so happened that as Don Quixote rode along amid all this acclaim, a Castilian who had read the sign on his back called out in a loud voice, "The devil take you for a Don Quixote of La Mancha! How is it you've made it this far without dying of the countless beatings that have rained down on your ribs? You are mad—and if you were mad in private and kept your madness to yourself, it would be less of an evil; but you have the knack of turning everyone who deals with you or talks with you into fools and blockheads. Just look at these gentlemen keeping you company! Go home, you idiot; look after your affairs, your wife, and your children, and give up this nonsense that's eating away your brain and skimming off your wits."

"Brother, go about your business," said Don Antonio, "and keep your advice for those who ask for it. Señor Don Quixote is entirely in his right mind, and we who accompany him are no fools; virtue deserves honor wherever it is found. Now be off with you, and bad luck go with you, and stop meddling where you're not wanted."

"By God, your worship is right," answered the Castilian, "because giving this good man advice is kicking against the goad; all the same, it makes me genuinely sad that the sound intelligence they say this blockhead has in every other matter should drain away down the channel of his knight-errantry. But may the bad luck your worship mentioned follow me and all my descendants if from this day forward—even if I live longer than Methuselah—I ever offer advice to anyone again, even if he begs me for it."

The advice-giver went on his way and the ride continued; but the crush of boys and townspeople pressing in to read the sign grew so great that Don Antonio had to take it off, pretending he was removing something else.

Night fell, they returned to the house, and there was a ladies' ball, for Don Antonio's wife—a woman of rank, high spirits, beauty, and wit—had invited some of her friends to come honor her guest and enjoy his extraordinary delusions. A good number came, they dined splendidly, and the dancing began at about ten o'clock. Among the ladies were two with a mischievous, playful streak who, while perfectly respectable, were rather free with their pranks when it came to harmless fun. These two were so relentless in dragging Don Quixote out to dance that they wore him down, not only in body but in spirit. He was a sight to behold—long, lank, lean, and sallow, his clothes plastered to his frame, awkward, and above all anything but light on his feet.

The merry ladies made sly advances to him, and he, just as slyly, rebuffed them; but finding himself hard pressed by their flirtations, he raised his voice and cried out, "_Fugite, partes adversæ!_ Leave me in peace, unwanted temptations! Away with your desires, ladies, for she who reigns as queen of mine, the peerless Dulcinea del Toboso, allows no desires but her own to take me captive and bring me low." And with that he sat down on the floor in the middle of the room, worn out and shattered by all his exertions in the dance.

Don Antonio ordered him carried bodily to bed, and the first to take hold of him was Sancho, saying as he did so, "It was an unlucky hour when you took up dancing, master of mine. Do you suppose every strong man of valor is a dancer, or every knight-errant given to cutting capers? If you do, I can tell you you're mistaken—there's many a man who'd sooner take on a giant than attempt a caper. Now if it had been the heel-stomp you were trying, I could stand in for you, because I can do the heel-stomp like a gerfalcon; but at proper dancing I'm useless."

With these remarks and others like them, Sancho set the whole ballroom laughing, and then he put his master to bed, tucking him in well so he could sweat out whatever chill he might have caught from his dancing.

The next day Don Antonio decided it was time to try out the enchanted head; and so, with Don Quixote, Sancho, two friends of his, and the two ladies who had danced Don Quixote into exhaustion at the ball—they had spent the night with Don Antonio's wife—he shut himself into the room where the head stood. He explained to them the power it possessed, swore them to secrecy, and told them that this was the first time he was going to test the enchanted head's virtue. Apart from Don Antonio's two friends, no one else was in on the trick of the enchantment—and even they, had Don Antonio not let them in on it beforehand, would inevitably have been struck with the same amazement as everyone else, so cleverly and skillfully was the thing contrived.

The first to put his mouth to the head's ear was Don Antonio himself, who said in a low voice—but not so low that everyone couldn't hear—"Head, tell me, by the power that lives in you: what am I thinking at this moment?"
Without any movement of its lips, the head answered in a clear, distinct voice that everyone could hear, "I do not judge thoughts."

Everyone was dumbstruck at this, all the more because there was no one near the table or anywhere in the room who could have spoken the answer. "How many of us are here?" Don Antonio asked next, and the reply came in the same soft tone: "You and your wife are here, with two friends of yours and two of hers, and a famous knight called Don Quixote of La Mancha, and a squire of his named Sancho Panza."

Now the astonishment broke out afresh; now everyone's hair stood on end with awe; and Don Antonio, stepping back from the head, exclaimed, "This is enough to convince me that the man who sold you to me did not cheat me, O wise head, talking head, answering head, marvelous head! Let someone else come forward and ask it whatever they like."

And since women are generally quick to act and curious by nature, the first to step up was one of the two friends of Don Antonio's wife, and her question was, "Tell me, Head, what must I do to be very beautiful?" The answer she received was, "Be very modest."
"I have no further questions for you," said the fair questioner.

Her companion came up next and said, "I should like to know, Head, whether my husband loves me or not." The answer she was given was, "Consider how he treats you, and you may judge for yourself." The married lady withdrew, saying, "That answer hardly needed a question; obviously the treatment a person receives reveals the feelings of the one who gives it."

Then one of Don Antonio's two friends stepped forward and asked, "Who am I?" "You know," came the answer. "That isn't what I'm asking," said the gentleman; "I'm asking whether you know me." "Yes, I know you—you are Don Pedro Noriz," was the reply.

"I need to know no more," said the gentleman, "for this alone convinces me, O Head, that you know everything." As he withdrew, the other friend approached and asked, "Tell me, Head, what does my eldest son want?"
"I have said already," came the answer, "that I do not judge wishes; nevertheless, I can tell you that what your son wishes is to bury you."
"That," said the gentleman, "is a case of 'what I see with my eyes I point out with my finger'—so I'll ask nothing further."

Don Antonio's wife came forward and said, "I don't know what to ask you, Head; I only want to learn from you whether I shall enjoy my good husband for many years." And the answer given her was, "You shall, for his health and his temperate way of living promise him many years of life, which so many others cut short through excess."

Then Don Quixote stepped up and said, "Tell me, you who answer: was what I describe as having happened to me in the cave of Montesinos the truth, or a dream? Will Sancho's whipping be carried through to the end without fail? Will the disenchantment of Dulcinea come to pass?"

"As for the matter of the cave," came the reply, "there is much to be said—it has something of both in it. Sancho's whipping will go forward at a leisurely pace. The disenchantment of Dulcinea will reach its proper completion."
"That is all I wish to know," said Don Quixote. "Let me only see Dulcinea disenchanted, and I will count all the good fortune I could ever desire as having come to me at a single stroke."

The last to ask was Sancho, and his questions were these: "Head, will I by any chance get another government? Will I ever escape this hard life of a squire? Will I ever get back to see my wife and children?" The answer came: "You shall govern in your own house; and if you return to it, you shall see your wife and children; and when you stop serving, you shall stop being a squire."
"Good, by God!" said Sancho Panza. "I could have told myself that much—the prophet Perogrullo couldn't have put it better."
"What kind of answer did you expect, you brute?" said Don Quixote. "Isn't it enough that the replies this head gives fit the questions it's asked?"
"Yes, it's enough," said Sancho, "but I'd have liked it to speak more plainly and tell me more."

The questions and answers ended there, but not the wonder that filled everyone except Don Antonio's two friends, who knew the secret. That secret Cide Hamete Benengeli chose to reveal at once, so as not to keep the world in suspense imagining that the head held some strange magical mystery. He says that Don Antonio, copying another head he had seen in Madrid, the work of an image-maker, built this one at home for his own amusement and to astound the ignorant; and its mechanism worked as follows. The tabletop was wood, painted and varnished to look like jasper, and the pedestal supporting it was of the same material, with four eagles' claws projecting from it to carry the weight more securely. The head, which looked like the bust or likeness of a Roman emperor and was tinted the color of bronze, was hollow all the way through, as was the tabletop, into which it was fitted so precisely that no seam could be seen where they joined. The table's pedestal was hollow as well and connected with the throat and neck of the head, and the whole apparatus communicated with another room directly beneath the chamber where the head stood. Running through the entire cavity—pedestal, table, throat, and neck of the bust or figure—was a tin tube, carefully fitted and hidden from view. In the room below, matching the one above, sat the person who was to give the answers, his mouth pressed to the tube; and the voice traveled, as through an ear-trumpet, from above downward and from below upward, the words arriving clear and distinct, so that the trick was impossible to detect. The answerer was a nephew of Don Antonio's, a sharp, quick-witted student; and since his uncle had told him in advance who would be coming into the chamber with him that day, it was easy for him to answer the first question promptly and accurately. The rest he answered by guesswork—and, being clever, he guessed cleverly. Cide Hamete adds that this marvelous device remained in operation for some ten or twelve days; but as word spread through the city that Don Antonio had in his house an enchanted head that answered everyone who questioned it, he grew afraid the news might reach the ears of the vigilant sentinels of our faith, and so he explained the matter to the inquisitors, who ordered him to dismantle it and be done with it, lest the ignorant masses be scandalized. In the opinion of Don Quixote and Sancho, however, the head remained an enchanted one, fully capable of answering questions—rather more to Don Quixote's satisfaction than to Sancho's.

The gentlemen of the city, to please Don Antonio, to do the honors for Don Quixote, and to give him an occasion for displaying his folly, arranged a tilting at the ring to be held six days later—which, however, for a reason that will be explained in due course, never took place.

Don Quixote felt like exploring the city quietly and on foot, fearing that if he went on horseback the boys would chase after him; so he and Sancho, with two servants Don Antonio provided, set out for a walk. As it happened, going down one of the streets, Don Quixote looked up and saw written in very large letters over a doorway, "Books printed here," which delighted him greatly, for he had never before seen a printing house and was curious to know what one was like. He went in with his whole retinue and watched them pulling sheets in one place, correcting proofs in another, setting type here, revising there—in short, all the operations to be seen in a great printing house. He approached one of the cases and asked what was being done there; the workmen explained, he watched in wonder, and moved on. Among others, he came up to one man and asked him what he was working on. The workman answered, "Señor, this gentleman here" (and he pointed to a man of pleasing appearance and a certain gravity of manner) "has translated an Italian book into our Spanish tongue, and I am setting it in type for the press."
"What is the book's title?" asked Don Quixote; to which the author replied, "Señor, in Italian the book is called _Le Bagatelle_."
"And what does _Le Bagatelle_ mean in our Spanish?" asked Don Quixote.
"_Le Bagatelle_," said the author, "is as if we were to say in Spanish _Los Juguetes_; but though the book carries a humble name, it contains good solid substance."

"I have a small smattering of Italian myself," said Don Quixote, "and I pride myself on singing a few of Ariosto's stanzas; but tell me, señor—and I say this not to test your ability but purely out of curiosity—have you ever come across the word _pignatta_ in your book?"
"Yes, many times," said the author.
"And how do you render it in Spanish?"
"How else would I render it," replied the author, "than by _olla_?"

"Good heavens," exclaimed Don Quixote, "what a master you are of the Italian language! I would wager good money that where the Italian says _piace_ you put _place_ in Spanish, and where it says _piu_ you put _mas_, and that you translate _sù_ as _arriba_ and _giù_ as _abajo_."
"Of course that's how I translate them," said the author, "since those are their proper equivalents."

"I would dare to swear," said Don Quixote, "that your worship is unknown to the world, which always begrudges its rewards to rare talents and praiseworthy labors. What abilities lie wasted there! What genius shoved into corners! What worth left to molder! Even so, it seems to me that translating from one language into another, unless it be from the queens of languages, Greek and Latin, is like looking at Flemish tapestries from the wrong side: the figures are visible, but they are clouded by threads that obscure them, and they lack the smooth, bright finish of the right side. And translating from easy languages shows no more wit or command of words than copying or transcribing one document from another. By this I don't mean to suggest that the work of translating deserves no credit, for a man could occupy himself in worse ways and ones less profitable to him. I leave out of this reckoning two famous translators: Doctor Cristóbal de Figueroa with his _Pastor Fido_ and Don Juan de Jáuregui with his _Aminta_, where each achieves such felicity that one cannot tell which is the translation and which the original. But tell me—are you printing this book at your own expense, or have you sold the rights to some bookseller?"
"I print at my own risk," said the author, "and I expect to clear at least a thousand ducats on this first edition, which will run to two thousand copies and sell out in no time at six reals apiece."

"A fine piece of arithmetic!" said Don Quixote. "It's obvious you don't know the tricks of the printers and the way they play into one another's hands. I promise you, when you find yourself burdened with two thousand copies, your body will ache in ways that will astonish you—especially if the book is at all unusual and not the least bit spicy."

"What!" said the author. "Would your worship have me hand it over to a bookseller who'll pay three maravedis for the rights and think he's doing me a kindness? I don't print my books to win fame in the world—my works have already made me known in it. I want profit; without it, reputation isn't worth a farthing."

"God grant your worship good fortune," said Don Quixote; and he moved on to another case, where he saw them correcting a sheet of a book entitled "Light of the Soul." Taking note of it, he remarked, "Books like this one, plentiful as they are, are the books that deserve printing, for the sinners nowadays are many, and infinite lights are needed for so many who walk in darkness."

He walked on and saw that they were also correcting another book; and when he asked its title, they told him it was called "The Second Part of the Ingenious Gentleman Don Quixote of La Mancha," by someone from Tordesillas.

"I've heard of this book already," said Don Quixote, "and truly, on my conscience, I thought it had been burned to ashes by now for its impertinence; but its Martinmas will come, as it comes to every pig. Invented stories are only as good and as delightful as they are close to the truth or the likeness of truth, and true ones are the better the truer they are." And so saying, with a flicker of irritation on his face, he walked out of the printing house. That same day Don Antonio arranged to take him to see the galleys anchored off the beach, which thrilled Sancho, who had never in his life seen any. Don Antonio sent word to the commandant of the galleys that he would be bringing his guest that afternoon—the famous Don Quixote of La Mancha, of whom the commandant and all the townspeople had already heard—to see them; and what happened aboard will be told in the following chapter.
